analysis.one_liner: Charges ranchers market-rate fees to graze livestock on federal public lands.
analysis.headline: The bill to charge ranchers fair-market grazing fees died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Ranchers pay far below market rates to graze cattle and sheep on national forest and Bureau of Land Management lands. This bill would have required the government to charge the fair market value of those grazing permits, set partly through competitive bidding, starting in 1996. Small family ranches earning modest incomes would have been exempt and kept the old low fee for ten years.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently subsidize below-market grazing on hundreds of millions of acres of public land; and wildlife, water quality, and public land users, because market-rate fees tend to reduce grazing pressure on fragile western lands. Small family ranches would have been shielded from the increase for a decade.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Secretaries of Agriculture and the Interior to set annual grazing fees equal to the fair market value of each lease or permit, based on what neighboring private land leases for and what services the government provides [S3].

It directs agencies to use competitive bidding to establish fair market value wherever practicable, which would end the practice of granting valuable public forage at politically set bargain rates [S3].

Small family ranches — those deriving most income from ranching, performing the labor themselves, and with incomes under $50,000 (or assets under $1 million) — could keep the old prevailing fee until 2006, limiting the hit on genuinely family-run operations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ranchers and large grazing-permit holders, who would pay substantially more for the exclusive use of federal land; in the near term the livestock industry would face higher costs, which could show up modestly in beef prices and squeeze some marginally profitable operations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Grazing permit holders on federal land

drawbacks.text: Raising fees to market rates would reduce the value of grazing permits, which ranchers currently hold as a capital asset, and could accelerate the consolidation of western ranching into larger operations if smaller permit holders exit the business despite the exemption [S3].

Higher grazing costs would eventually flow into livestock producers' expenses, with some pass-through to consumers in meat prices, and would reduce the income base of rural communities dependent on federal grazing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The subsidy being ended is narrow — it benefits a few thousand western grazing-permit holders while costing taxpayers money and contributing to overgrazing on public land. The ten-year small-family exemption answers the strongest fairness objection, though it cannot prevent some consolidation in the ranching economy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Resources Committee and then to its National Parks subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on January 25, 1995, and it was referred to the House Committee on Resources [S5].
Six days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Lands, with executive comment requested from the Interior Department and USDA [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a subcommittee or committee vote and never reached the House floor before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Grazing-permit holders and the livestock industry are better off, since they continue grazing federal land at below-market fees that taxpayers effectively subsidize.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Livestock grazers keeping their federal subsidy

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require fair-market-value grazing fees and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 14 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (13 Democrats and 1 Independent).

against.name: Rep. Don Young
against.what_they_did: His committee referred the bill to a subcommittee and never reported it out, so it never received a hearing or vote.

against.name: Livestock and grazing industry groups
against.what_they_did: Long-standing opponents of grazing fee increases, which would multiply what their members pay to use federal forage.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no votes or floor debate; the bill's 15 supporters were almost all Democrats, and the Republican-led Resources Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have replaced below-market federal grazing fees with fair-market rates and competitive bidding, ending a subsidy that ranchers receive at public expense. A decade-long exemption shielded small family ranches, but large permit holders would have paid sharply more.
Federal grazing programs have long cost more to administer than they collect in fees; market-rate fees would have moved toward recovering those costs. Ordinary taxpayers bear the difference today.
